I just watched Transformers for the first time, and I genuinely thought it was terrible. I know this movie has a massive fanbase and was hugely successful, but I honestly struggle to understand the appeal. For most of the runtime, it just felt like a constant barrage of explosions, screaming, fighting, cars, robots and things flying across the screen. Something is always happening, but somehow I still found it incredibly unengaging. The biggest problem for me was the plot. I know you’re supposed to just accept the concept of alien robots coming to Earth and disguising themselves as cars, but even within that setup, the story felt unnecessarily convoluted and ridiculous. Everyone is chasing the same objects, different groups keep appearing, robots are fighting robots, the military gets involved, and eventually it all just becomes noise. The dialogue also really didn’t work for me. So many lines felt unbelievably cheesy, to the point where I was genuinely uncomfortable at times. The humor, the dramatic speeches, the romantic scenes, the military dialogue – almost everything has this extremely specific mid-2000s blockbuster cheesiness to it. And I like Shia LaBeouf in plenty of other movies, but even he couldn’t really save this for me. There wasn’t a character, relationship or storyline that I felt particularly invested in. The one thing I can absolutely give the movie credit for is the visual effects. Especially considering this came out in 2007, the Transformers themselves still look impressive. The transformations are incredibly detailed, the CGI interacts convincingly with the real environments, and I can imagine that seeing this on a huge cinema screen at the time probably felt pretty revolutionary. But great effects aren’t enough for me when I don’t care about anything that’s happening around them. It also feels incredibly representative of a certain kind of American blockbuster from that era: huge cars, military hardware, attractive people, explosions, loud music and everything constantly turned up to eleven. I can see how that spectacle appealed to a massive audience, especially in 2007, but it really isn’t for me. By the end I genuinely felt exhausted rather than entertained. There’s very little here that made me think about the movie afterwards beyond wondering how something this loud could somehow still bore me. I’m definitely not a Transformers fan, and this movie certainly didn’t turn me into one. The effects are impressive, but almost everything else – the dialogue, the characters, the plot and the nonstop action – did absolutely nothing for me. I will not be watching this again.

2.5/10 "The first Transformers is actually kinda good." That's a sentence I've heard loads of times. I have no idea what's going on in the minds of the people who say that. The first Transformers is one of the most embarrassing AAA productions I know of. And it only goes downhill from here. The entire movie's attitude is just loathsome. It tries to mash a few dark and serious elements together with dialogue and comic relief straight out of a frat house. Every character is unbelievably obnoxious. I don't understand why anyone would ever want to follow these people, or why anyone would ever care about anything that's happening. The entire world this film takes place in is insufferable, and the whole thing feels like it was made by a bunch of college jocks. Everything about it is just annoying. It's also weird how often the movie seems to be attempting some kind of parody of the American government. The directing is actually okay for a production like this. The blend of on-set footage and CGI works great, and Bay directs the actors competently. What I do find hilarious, however, is just how clearly his background in music video directing shines through in quite a few shots. That - and especially how aggressively everything is geared towards being cool and badass - comes off as incredibly cringe and try-hard. Ninety per cent of the story is made up of some lame McGuffin fetch quest with stakes I couldn't care less about, because the world and the characters suck. And it all eventually culminates in one of the least exciting third acts I've ever seen. There's battle scene after battle scene, but not only do I barely know what's going on because half the Transformers look the same, I also don't really care. It's just more and more fighting, and I realised that watching Transformers transform into and out of cars had already gotten boring the third time around. This film is filled to the brim with stupid shit and is, in general, one of the most unenjoyable ways to spend two hours and fifteen minutes that I can think of.

Some say that he makes good first entries and that he always finds a place for spectacle. All I know is that this movie sucks. While the story between Sam (Shia LaBeouf) and Bumblebee (Mark Ryan) can be a grounding moment, it isn’t enough force to get it on land. Neither is Peter Cullen’s performance as Optimus Prime, the score, or the fights. Optimus owing his life to Sam does make sense though and Optimus says his iconic lines and good new lines. But that’s just about where the fun ends. First, Michael Bay doesn’t seem to respect the lore for Cybertron is supposed to be habitable, at least for the Decepticons. There’s too many subplots, the wrong tone with the military and disaster film aspects, too detailed CGI with the Decepticons being all gray, too much human stuff, bad jokes, especially Bumblebee and the lubricant and Ratchet (Robert Foxworth) saying Sam’s pheromone levels suggests he wants to have a kid with Mikaela (Megan Fox). Also the whole Sam selling his great-grandfather’s glasses on eBay is meaningless. Shia LaBeouf is just alright as Sam, he tries, but Bay, Roberto Orci, and Alex Kurtzman don’t give him much to work with. So little that Sam doesn’t feel like a hero as he’s given no space to grow into one. Megan Fox is also not impressive as she is subjected to Bay sexualizing her, even when doing something as simple as looking into what’s wrong with a car. Although that’s more so how she is dressed. Bay and Fox have history, as she was portrayed at 15 quite suggestively in Bad Boys II (2003), and Fox did not forget that. This movie doesn’t feel like a step in the right direction with Fox in Bay’s movies. Especially since she doesn’t have much of a character and is mostly here so Bay can feature the male gaze. Dwelling on humans unfortunately means Optimus and Megatron (Hugo Weaving) don’t appear until an hour in, and Megatron is not an active threat until the movie is nearly over. Speaking of Megatron, Weaving is nothing impressive. If they brought back Frank Welker, who voiced Megatron in G1 to pair with Cullen’s Optimus, it may have been more believable that these two had history. Weaving can act, he was good as Red Skull, but he can’t really in this movie. Speaking of the actual Transformers, Bumblebee having no lines gives him no character and we also don’t see him take the form of the 2007 Camaro. Jazz dying without any investment in his character is straight up shrewd. So now I’ve gotten past the problems with the characters. Does that mean the story’s good? I wish the answer was “Yes”. First, revisionist history opens a flood of confusion. The Hoover Dam was built due to the Cube (and the AllSpark) being there? And the two worlds have met before? So why then do the humans pretend they don’t know what’s happening? If none of the revisionist history was here and the events of the movie were the first time Cybertron’s inhabitants met humans on Earth, it would be a much cleaner story. Second, it takes too long to get to what really matters. It takes like 45 minutes to an hour to get to what matters, the Decepticons want the Cube and the Autobots can’t let that happen. Because of the human stuff, it prevents us from just cutting to the chase. Overall, a first entry that could have been worse, but does not provide encouragement for what’s next. 3/10 or 1½ stars.

Steve Jablonsky's score is masterful, and it works with Peter Cullen and Hugo Weaving's incredible voice acting to bring real solemnity to the sweeping, tragic tale of Cybtertron's fall. I think at this point, it doesn't even matter if I don't think this is a good movie and I gave it 2 stars. Rating Michael Bay's Transformers 2007 is meaningless. It has transcended criticism and entered into the hallowed halls of our cultural memory.

Every character in this film is a dickhead. Racist soldiers on the chopper? Dickheads. Spike Witwicky hawking his family airlooms for a car? Dickhead.  Spike Witwicky abandoning his friend at the lake? Double dickhead. Dad Witwicky taking his son to the Porsche garage? Dickhead. Mum Witwicky obsessed about her son gooning? Dickhead. Optimus Prime? Dickhead. Ironhide? Dickhead. John Turturro? Dickhead. Meghan Fox? Actually, not a dickhead, so Michael Bay got rid of her. There is something profoundly off in the writing of this movie. I feel it's like colourblind people trying to describe a colour they've never seen; in this case, it's facsimiles of human beings trying to write American teenagers and their relationships having only devoured other films about the topic. But there's something more than that - after all, Tarantino has made a career from refashioning the obsessions of his youth (and Bumblebee does a similar thing with more love and panache) - there's something profoundly off about all of the human characters in this film. It's vexing - if it had been slightly more surreal it might have ended up an almost Lynchian take on the psychosexual underbelly of teenage popular discourse, but we've arrived  here in this weird place by  accident, as jock writers do their best to embody pop cultural tropes that grow more distorted the more they are photocopied. But look, against my better judgement, once the movie stops pretending to be a John Hughes' dog in heat, it gets better. ILM absolutely smash the ball out the park and the back half is tight. I can just imagine Bay and the head of ILM doing that Arnold hand clasp from Predator before hitting the open air gym at Venice Beach once they'd locked the movie. Even though there are better live action versions of this that are roughly the same story (Bumblebee), movies that are just leagues better (TF:One, the original 86 film) and TV shows that have more pathos in their little cybertronian finger than this entire film (Animated, Prime, Seasons two and three of Cyberverse) I will admit that this is a singular vision, and you could not mistake it for the work of anyone else. I wish I had a polarizing take on Transformers (2007), but as a product of the 2000s, this had little impact on my life at a time that it very well could have. Some Michael Bay enthusiasts I know are unapologetically in love with the Transformers franchise, and I'll admit that I see the appeal. This is a bombastic, explosive, ten-toes-down blockbuster with commentary about military, police, and humanity, and it looks pretty great while doing it... but similarly to some of the Americanized Godzilla films, while I had a good time with this one, it failed to leave much of a lasting impression on me. I will give the film credit for its action sequences; it's over-the-top and impressive in its blockbuster filmmaking, especially for 2007. The CGI holds up refreshingly well, and the cliches aren't executed haphazardly. I think part of the disconnect comes from a lack of literacy in Bay's filmography, which I plan to rectify sooner rather than later, but I also struggle to reconcile that with the lack of humanity in the human characters. I found the Transformers themselves infinitely more interesting than Sam, Mikaela, or any of the other human characters. Sure, that's somewhat to be expected in the Transformers movie, but this 144-minute action extravaganza spent enough time on the humans to give me more meaningful time with them or more depth to the Transformers. I suppose I can find more of that in the next three films. Ultimately, I think there's room for me to appreciate this more on rewatch, but this is good, not great to my tastes as of today.

Maybe it's that there's just a lot going on or that the camera is always shaking: it doesn't matter, the decepticons, the autobots, and everything in between look probably exactly how you'd want them to look in a live-action film. I grew up watching Transformers as a kid, and I was completely into it. I had all the little robot toys, and I can still remember having fun transforming them and playing with them while watching the cartoon. So when this movie came out, there was definitely a part of me that was excited to see these characters brought to the big screen. And honestly, Transformers delivers pretty well on that childhood nostalgia. Seeing Optimus Prime, Bumblebee, Megatron, Starscream and the rest of the Transformers brought to life with modern special effects was pretty damn cool. The designs and transformations felt like a natural evolution of what I remembered from the cartoon, and the movie actually captures a lot of the spirit of what made the original series fun. Watching these giant robots transform, fight and tear up the screen is exactly the kind of thing younger me would have loved. As an adult, though, I can also see the movie’s flaws. The story isn’t anything groundbreaking, some of the human characters and comedy don’t always work for me, and at times it feels more like a showcase for the special effects than a great story. But I never really expected Transformers to be some deep cinematic experience. I wanted to have fun with it, and that’s exactly what I got. The action is entertaining, the effects still hold up pretty well, and there’s something satisfying about seeing characters I grew up with finally getting the big-budget treatment. Is it the best movie I’ve ever seen? Definitely not. Is it a bad movie? Not at all. For me, Transformers is simply a fun, nostalgic ride that brought a piece of my childhood back to the big screen.

An engaging blockbuster overall, but definitely one that loses itself its the final act. Starting off with its thrilling political intrigue, espionage, and military action, Transformers hooks you from the start with its brisk pace. LaBeouf is brilliant as Sam, flawlessly conveying his nerdy and comedic traits. The CGI’s thoroughly impressive, though they lack the holistic perspective of later films (not exactly a flaw). The character designs are brilliant (save perhaps Megatron), with the original lineup of Autobots and Decepticons being highly distinct from their respective groups. The action is fun for the most part, but certainly not as innovative or prominent as in later instalments. While Bumblebee received a major focus, I certainly wish Optimus had more screen time. Unfortunately, flaws are prevalent in the film’s middle and final acts. The Autobots hiding outside Sam’s home is cute at first, but quickly becomes obnoxious. The initial sequences with Sector 7 are largely uninteresting, hindering the previously thrilling pace. As for the final act, action sequences with the actual Transformers are brief. The overall resolution is abrupt, with Megatron feeling dumbed down for the sake of it. Still iconic, but lacks the action the Bayverse is known for. I don’t know how, but the military propaganda in Bay’s initial trilogy just works. And that ending scene is just legendary

Absolutely a propaganda movie about the US military, but it’s so worth the watch. Transformers (2007) is one of those movies that the whole family can enjoy. Action, comedy, romance, it has everything. Shia LaBeouf has a career defining performance as Sam. He’s smart, funny, and logical. At first it seems he’s a basic nerd who wants the girl, but he is shown to be witty and sincere. In the ocean of solid performances, there are a few that reach his watchability. Omar Benson Miller bashing through the glass window and getting tackled into the pool. Anthony Anderson and the donuts. Josh Duhamel as a stereotypical but affable soldier. Kevin Dunn and Julie White as probably the most enjoyable movie parents I’ve ever seen. And of course, Peter Cullen (rip) as the infamous Optimus Prime. This movie lays a foundation of a trilogy that would rock the late 2000’s family living room. Also, for me, this put Linkin Park on the map of everyone else who wasn’t already fans of the band. Michael Bay nails this movie in the most Michael Bay way.

In memory of Peter Cullen, I've decided to watch and complete this movie finally. What a solid fun action movie. It's silly, it's fun, it's hype, it's peak. The simple story of the Autobots protecting the cube while the Decepticons try to retrieve it is compelling enough and it works for this movie. The protagonist, Sam, is a flawed but fun protagonist who ends up saving the day in the end cause like it's aura and he becomes a true hero, which was great to see. Megan Fox as Mikaela was great as well, the chemistry between her and our protagonist worked well especially standing out in the first half of the movie. The military guys were cool too, there was one part where one of the guys genuinely risked his life for the clip I loved it. And of course the Transformers themselves were great, showing each of their personalities in a simple but effective way. The Transformers looked great especially for 2007 standards and of course they had tons of hype moments and aura. Optimus with his speeches, Megatron with his aura one liners, Bumblebee with his playfulness and the rest of them with their guns and ammo. During the action scenes in this film, you can genuinely turn your brain off and let your eyes enjoy while during the other scenes, the simple yet effective story progression and comedy is fulfilling.
